p.src: I once assembled six works of genius: the Zhuangzi, the Songs of Chu, Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian, Du Fu’s regulated verse, Water Margin, and The Western Wing. I presumptuously added my critical annotations and revisions, and discerning gentlemen throughout the realm approved of me as one who understood literature. Recently I read the Romance of the Three Kingdoms and found that it sets forth events on the basis of fact, rather than fabricating them from fancy, and may therefore stand as a complement to the Classics and histories. Seen in this light, no work is more extraordinary than the Three Kingdoms. Someone may ask: “From the Zhou and Qin down through the Han and Tang and afterward, every historical romance derived from the chronicles resembles the Three Kingdoms. Why single it out as extraordinary?” I reply: “The Three Kingdoms constituted one of the most extraordinary struggles for dominion in all history; and the author who dramatized those kingdoms was likewise one of the most extraordinary masters of fiction in all history. Struggles for dominion in other ages were comparatively commonplace, and those who made narratives from them employed comparatively pedestrian art; hence they cannot remotely be placed beside the Three Kingdoms.”

p.src: I have contemplated the contest of the Three Kingdoms for all under Heaven and marveled that the transformations wrought by destiny truly lie beyond all fathoming. When Emperor Xian of Han lost his authority, Dong Zhuo usurped power, heroes rose on every side, and the whole realm seethed like a boiling cauldron. Had Imperial Uncle Liu early enjoyed the perfect accord of fish and water with his counselor, first secured Jingzhou and Xiangyang, driven north across the Yellow River, sent proclamations through Huainan and Jiangdong, and subdued Qin and Yong in succession, the result would merely have been another restoration like that of Emperor Guangwu, and destiny’s genius for change would never have appeared. Yet Dong Zhuo failed in his usurpation and was put to death, whereupon Cao Cao gained the power to coerce the Son of Heaven and command the feudal lords. Though imperial title and rank had become hollow, the legitimate calendar had not yet changed. Imperial Uncle Liu wandered from place to place, fleeing adversity, and could not proclaim the great cause to the realm at an early hour; meanwhile, the lands north and south of the Yangzi had already been seized by Wu and Wei, leaving only one corner in the southwest where the house of Liu might set foot. Yet had Kongming not emerged to aid the battle at Red Cliffs in the east and later strike a crushing blow in Hanzhong to the west, the regions of Han and Yi would also have fallen to Cao Cao, and Wu could not have remained independent. The outcome would then have been another usurpation of Han like Wang Mang’s, and destiny’s genius for change would still have remained unseen. But after Cao Cao escaped at Huarong and returned from the campaign he dismissed as “chicken ribs,” the three powers stood like the legs of a cauldron, matched in authority and strength, and the tripartite balance was at last formed. Consider Cao Cao’s entire life: his crimes overflowed their measure, and gods and men alike raged against him. He was denounced in proclamations, reviled, stabbed, poisoned, burned, raided; his beard was cut, his teeth broken, he fell from his horse and tumbled into a ditch. Many times he came close to death, yet in the end escaped it. His enemies were numerous, but so too were his supporters. It was as though Heaven deliberately meant to establish the tripartite realm and therefore preserved this treacherous hero to remain a scourge upon Han. Moreover, Heaven brought forth Zhou Yu as a match for Zhuge Liang, and then Sima Yi to succeed the house of Cao; it was as if Heaven feared that one leg of the tripod might break and repeatedly produced men of talent to hold one another in check. There have been divided regimes since antiquity, and there have been kings ruling separate domains: the Twelve States, the Seven States, the Sixteen Kingdoms, the Northern and Southern Dynasties, the Eastern and Western Wei, and the Former and Later Han. Amid them, power was gained one moment and lost the next; some states perished while others survived. At most they failed to endure twelve years, and at the shortest they lasted no more than months. Never before, across sixty years, did three powers rise together and perish together in so extraordinary a struggle for the realm as that of the Three Kingdoms. The marvels of this book are enough to delight learned scholars when they read it, and equally to delight the unlettered folk of humble lanes; heroes and champions delight in reading it, and ordinary men of the world delight in it as well.

p.src: Long ago, when Kuai Tong counseled Han Xin, he had already proposed a tripartite division balanced like the legs of a cauldron. At the time, however, Han Xin had already become a subject of Han and could not in righteousness betray it; Xiang Yu was brutal and lacked foresight, and though he had one Fan Zeng, he could not employ him. The realm therefore could not but be unified by the Han, where all joined their wisdom and strength. The possibility of a tripartite realm appeared as an empty portent when the house of Han was first ascending, but was finally realized when that house had fallen into decline. Moreover, Gaozu rose as King of Han, while the First Sovereign brought Han to its end: the one recovered and pacified the Three Qin, while the other could not take a single inch of the Central Plain. It seems that blue Heaven, in creating Han, had already ordained in the unseen that it should begin in this fashion and end in the same: thus the people and events of that age, each with distinctive talent and strategy, entered circumstances uniquely their own and became utterly unlike those of all other ages. Is this not the greatest marvel wrought by Heaven?

p.src: The author of the Romance transmitted extraordinary events through extraordinary prose. Moreover, he had no need to indulge in strained invention: he merely linked the facts, interweaving their beginnings and endings, and nothing failed to become marvelous. This too is a feat of human art never witnessed before. Yet though the events are extraordinary and the book extraordinary, no one had arisen to criticize and annotate it. Even if such a person appeared, unless he possessed a brocade heart and an embroidered tongue, and could voice every hidden intention of the ancients in their stead, this book would in the end remain on the same level as the many historical romances from before the Zhou and Qin and after the Han and Tang. How, then, could anyone recognize its marvels and believe in them? I once wished to explore its marvels and reveal their true worth to the world, but illness prevented me from accomplishing the task. Then suddenly, upon a friend’s desk, I saw Master Mao’s manuscript commentary on the Romance of the Three Kingdoms. Observing the exhilaration of his brushwork and the acuity of his thought, I found that he had grasped before me precisely what my own heart affirmed. Twice I cried out in delight. From this day forward, I know that the title “First Work of Genius” does indeed belong to the Three Kingdoms. I have therefore written these few words as a preface, to be placed at the head of the volume when Master Mao entrusts it to the engraver, so that later readers may know that Master Mao and I are of one mind.
